title: SEBI's PMS Rule Review Puts NRI Investment Barriers in the Spotlight
excerpt: India's portfolio management industry has grown to ₹10.5 lakh crore, but overseas Indians remain locked out by onboarding friction and regulatory complexity. SEBI's first rule overhaul since 2020 could change that.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • SEBI is reviewing PMS regulations for the first time since 2020, with a consultation paper expected soon.
  • India's PMS industry manages ₹10.5 lakh crore, but NRI participation remains low despite high remittances.
  • Onboarding challenges, including complex regulations and costs, hinder NRI investments from the US and Canada.
  • Budget 2026 doubled NRI investment limits, but new account openings remain minimal, indicating limited impact.

India's portfolio management services industry has a $143.6 billion question: why does almost none of it come from overseas Indians?

The Securities and Exchange Board of India is now revisiting that question as it undertakes its first full review of PMS regulations since 2020. SEBI Chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey announced the review in February, initially targeting a June timeline. Deliberations have extended into July, according to Moneycontrol, with a consultation paper expected soon.

A Booming Industry With a Blind Spot

The numbers tell a split story. PMS assets under management — excluding EPFO and provident fund assets — have grown from roughly ₹5 trillion in FY21 to ₹10.5 trillion as of January 2026, a compounded annual growth rate of around 17%. The client base has crossed 2.15 lakh, up nearly 50% since 2022, and the number of registered portfolio managers has risen from 361 to 501.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=5KrRjnlTYrU

But that growth has been almost entirely domestic. Industry participants estimate NRI investors contribute only a low single-digit share of PMS assets — a striking gap given that India's inward remittances touched $143.6 billion in FY26, up 16.3% year-on-year, according to RBI data. For the first time, advanced economies led by the United States overtook the Gulf as India's largest source of remittances, with the US alone contributing 27.7% of the total.

"NRI contributions have evolved from primarily remittance-based support for families to sophisticated, return-seeking portfolio and direct investments."

— Ashok Kumar, Senior Vice President and Head – Advisory, Scripbox

The Onboarding Wall

The core complaint from industry executives is not the investment cap — it is what happens before an NRI can invest at all. Opening a PMS account typically requires a demat account and, in many cases, a dedicated NRI bank account. Each is governed by a different regulator, involving RBI and IFSCA coordination, embassy attestation that can cost roughly $100 per set of documents, physical signatures, and hard-copy paperwork designed for investors sitting in India.

Several PMS providers still refuse to onboard NRI clients based in the United States and Canada, citing FATCA compliance complexity. That effectively locks out India's most financially capable diaspora segment.

"These are investors who manage sophisticated portfolios in their countries of residence and are looking for the same rigour when deploying capital back home," said Tanvi Kancchan, Head of Strategy at Anand Rathi Shares & Stock Brokers. "PMS offers exactly that: direct ownership, professional management and full transparency. The product is right; what remains is making the access genuinely frictionless."

Budget 2026 Moved the Limit, Not the Needle

Budget 2026 doubled the individual NRI investment limit in listed Indian companies from 5% to 10% and strengthened the Portfolio Investment Scheme. The Association of Portfolio Managers in India (APMI) welcomed the step, with chairman Biharilal Deora calling PMS route announcements for persons resident outside India "a great example of such an enabler."

But wealth management executives advising NRI clients say the ground reality has not shifted. One executive told Moneycontrol the impact "isn't significant," adding: "The first indication can be revealed from how many newer accounts have been opened. Not substantial."

NRI Investment Challenges
›Onboarding requires multiple regulators and documents.
›Costs for embassy attestation can reach $100.
›FATCA compliance complicates onboarding for US-based NRIs.
›Many PMS providers refuse to onboard NRIs from the US and Canada.

The broader regulatory environment, however, is evolving. The RBI released draft Foreign Exchange Management (Foreign Investment) Rules, 2026 last week, proposing a more streamlined framework for foreign investment. Separately, plans are under consideration to allow NRIs and overseas citizens of India to subscribe to the National Pension System with repatriable benefits — part of a wider push to attract stable, long-term foreign capital rather than short-term portfolio flows.

What APMI Wants From the Review

APMI says it has worked with SEBI for four years on regulatory feedback and has submitted a global benchmarking study comparing India's framework with other jurisdictions. Its recommendations include facilitating global capital flows via an NRI/PROI framework, adapting PMS for larger global wealth trends, and simplifying business operations for both investors and managers.

The association is also pushing SEBI to address longstanding pain points: the requirement to open a fresh demat account when switching portfolio managers, which creates operational and tax complications, and the lack of a single-window digital onboarding process.

India's tax treatment of NRI portfolio investments also lags rival hubs. Industry voices suggest extending GIFT City-style tax treatment more broadly to NRI capital rather than confining favourable treatment to one financial enclave.

Lessons From Other Diasporas

Budget 2026: A Missed Opportunity?
›NRI investment limit in listed companies doubled from 5% to 10%.
›Industry executives report minimal new account openings.
›Regulatory changes aim to attract stable foreign capital.
›APMI calls for simplified onboarding processes.

India is not the only country trying to channel diaspora capital into formal investment. Israel has raised more than $40 billion since 1951 through diaspora bonds, aided by registering with the US SEC to access American retail investors — a step India has deliberately avoided to sidestep US regulatory burdens. The Philippines has taken a digital-first approach, with its state-backed Overseas Filipino Bank serving clients across 130 countries through an app-based model.

Both examples suggest the same conclusion: reducing friction and building diaspora-specific digital rails matters as much as headline investment limits or tax rates. Whether SEBI's review will deliver that kind of structural change remains to be seen, but the consultation paper — now the industry's most-watched regulatory document — should clarify its direction.
